Cape Epic Storms

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The worst storm to hit the Cape since 1984 devastates life and limb

Unique Selling Point:
Nine people have died in Cape Town and 3 so far in raging fires around Knysna -- the Defence Force has been called in to help contain the fire and ensure that evacuees are safe. We track the devastatation being left in the wake of the storm - from Cape Town to Knysna and Plettenberg Bay and see how the Cape has rallied to deal with the tragedy of several storm-related deaths.

Press Release:


Cape weather storms and the Knysna blaze
Up to 10 000 people were forced to evacuate their homes as fires fuelled by strong winds ripped through the sleepy town of Knysna. Scores of
homes have been gutted and several buildings destroyed in what’s been called one of the worst disasters to hit the town in decades. Further
across the province, dramatic weather patterns have brought raging storms to the Mother City, wreaking havoc and leaving thousands
homeless


Script:


SCRIPT: Cape Epic Storm
TX DATE: 11 June 2017
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: John Webb

(11 secs) This is all that’s left of large parts of the tourist town Knysna. Hundreds of firefighters came to battle the devouring wildfires raging from Wednesday, fueled by strong, warm berg winds.

(11 secs) One after another, Garden Route towns caught alight -- Mossel Bay, Plettenberg Bay, Oudtshoorn -- on Saturday, George and Port Elizabeth awoke to flames. The N2 was closed in the firestorm.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: We had several other fire teams coming, City of Cape Town Centre’s fire team...Mossel Bay was here, but had to withdraw because their own fire started.
(3 secs) Knysna municipality spokesperson Fran Kirsten.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: But of course, as you know, the weather never abated. The wind kept blowing. The Air Force was on standby the entire time, but they could not be mobilised and when the wind stopped yesterday, they took to the air and they started bombing.
(4 secs) Firefighter Leeroy Baatjies knows the odds when fighting against the wind.
LEEROY BAATJIES, SEDGEFIELD FIREFIGHTER: We’ve been here on this fire from this morning. We, we met the fire in Uniondale. We are currently busy with the line, just making sure there’s no flare-ups again to cause another fire.
(6 secs) This piece of melted glass was Louis Jordaan’s sliding front door, until the early hours of Wednesday morning.
(6 min) This was his neighbour’s brand new television set and washing machine.
LOUIS JORDAAN, KNYSNA RESIDENT: They were very shocked because the fire was furious. I’ve been wearing these clothes for four days now...I have nothing else, they still smell of smoke.The most important thing for me was to try to save other people’s lives and to save children above all.
(8 sec) Across Knysna’s valleys, in an upmarket golf estate, Niall O’Hagan was called back from work at two in the afternoon.
NIALL O’HAGAN, KNYSNA RESIDENT: We literally got out of here as the… as the flames were coming across the road. It’s amazing how some houses missed the fire and some houses are intact as you will see that one up over there. But these two were directly in the path…
(4 secs) Danielle Pieters runs the equestrian centre at the Oakhill School.
DANIELLE PIETERS, OAKHILL SCHOOL EQUESTRIAN CENTRE: We thought that we would escape the path of the fire, but it unbelievably jumped the river behind us, but within 10 minutes our stables, our hay barns, our tack rooms, everything had burned completely to the ground and we were surrounded by flames...they surrounded us and the 35 horses that live here but they didn’t manage to get to us.
(7 secs) Over 600 properties have been reduced to rubble and ash.
JOHN LINK: A thick blanket of smoke and shocked silence hung over Knysna in the aftermath of the fire. It devastated massive areas of vegetation and displaced thousands of people. And for the residents the question is not when but how they begin to pick up the pieces.
(4 sec) Very little is left of Craig Patterson’s family home.
CRAIG PATTERSON, KNYSNA RESIDENT: When I came back from work, I came around the…the first bend when you come into Salt River and as you come around the bend, from seeing nothing we’re coming around the bend, I thought like a volcano going off because like sparks jumping and shooting, you know. Very scary. So, ja, then I got on the phone. No, don’t worry, the family is all been taken to the church, they’re all safe. I couldn’t believe how fast fire can actually move.
(14 sec) As people fled burning homes, the Vineyard Church became a makeshift relief centre that’s now been running 96 hours straight -- pastors Dee-Anne Olivier, her husband Steve and an army of volunteers coordinate donations streaming in from around the country.
DEE-ANNE OLIVIER, KNYSNA PASTOR: The telephone poles were all being burned so people couldn’t communicate with each other. We had a lot of families separated because the N2 was closed because of the fires. My own family, we were evicted four times...well, evacuated four times throughout the night as every place we went to, the ash just started following us and the flames were coming after us.
JOHN LINK: There’s a hypothetical question that asks what we would save in the event of a fire. But for the people of Knysna, things happened so quickly, that wasn’t even a consideration.
(6 secs) And that’s after warnings of a severe storm front and high pressure system that would bring driving winds had been received...
DEE-ANNE OLIVIER, KNYSNA PASTOR: We were in warning about the storm that was coming, but we didn’t, we were expecting rain and wind. We weren’t expecting fires.
(7 secs) Capetonians were first to be hit by the predicted storm’s gale-force winds and huge waves. About a hundred people lost their homes.
DR PETER JOHNSTON, AFRICAN CLIMATE & DEVELOPMENT INITIATIVE, UCT: The thing that separates a bad storm from a regular storm is the wind speed.
(5 secs) Dr Peter Johnston is a climate scientist at the University of Cape Town.
DR PETER JOHNSTON, AFRICAN CLIMATE & DEVELOPMENT INITIATIVE, UCT: We could see from the satellite pictures and the pressure systems this was going to be a strong wind and the winds did gust over 100 kilometres an hour. And we saw the trees were blown down and we saw car blown over and trucks blown over. So it was a severe storm.
(21 secs) Trees were uprooted and power lines downed across the city. Roofs were blown off in various informal settlements and low-income areas. A 60-year-old man died in Lavender Hill when a wall collapsed on his wendy house. In Imizamo Yethu in Hout Bay, residents who are still rebuilding after a devastating shack fire in March, have now been hit by flooding and wind damage.
JOHN LINK: Cape Town is currently experiencing one of its worst ever droughts. So no wonder people here were hoping that this week’s storm would bring some form of relief. Sadly, though, the storm was more about wind than rain.
DR PETER JOHNSTON, AFRICAN CLIMATE & DEVELOPMENT INITIATIVE, UCT: We know that the water did fall on the dams and fall in the catchment area of the dams and we’re hoping that the dams will have filled up maybe 5% in a storm like this. It’s going to take a long time for the dams to fill, it’s not going to happen in one storm.
(11 secs) The same wind that whipped the Cape coast, fanned the fires that continue to flare up across the Southern Cape. Already drought-stricken, Knysna has now been declared a disaster area.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: Before this we were in level 3, which meant that we had 27 days of water left. Now with the fire and the fire fighting efforts, human life was first, so the water got used for that.
JOHN LINK: It can be incredibly difficult to find any sort of consolation in tragedies such as these. But if there is a silver lining for the residents off Knysna, it’s in the way that people from elsewhere have come together to contribute to the humanitarian process.
(15 secs) Churches, municipalities, Gift of the Givers, the Red Cross...everyone is standing by with crisis relief. It’s not yet been possible to accurately determine how many people were left homeless -- but in Knysna 20 suburbs in all were evacuated.
LOUIS JORDAAN, KNYSNA RESIDENT: It really hurts. We are sleeping in a school, we have pregnant women, women with 2-month old babies who are sleeping on the cement floor...you cannot say a sponge is a proper bed, it’s literally cement. Its very painful seeing people sleeping on the cement floor...we also sleep in other people’s houses, sleeping on chairs because there are no beds.
(13 secs) The death toll stands at five -- including a family of three who were overcome by smoke while trying to flee. A young volunteer firefighter died in hospital after suffering burn wounds. Police have no proof that any fires were set on purpose.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: So far we have no idea. As we say was within forestry hamlet. So it wasn’t within the town, it wasn’t within the township. We have no idea yet. The most… right now, all we’re doing is trying to save lives, structures, cause and all that and how much damage was done, will be done once the mopping up process happens and that will start once the fire is out.
(7 secs) Relief workers say the greatest need at the moment is for non-perishable food, especially baby food, warm blankets and matresses.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: We’re all a little overwhelmed. Now that we know human life is safe and we don’t have the fear of people dying...it’s just, this can’t happen.
CRAIG PATTERSON, KNYSNA RESIDENT: Very emotional. But ja, you know. I’m going to try get things going here again and ja, you know. There is a… that small little section over there, actually got walls and a door. So at least I can get one room going and then slowly start to go again. A lot of hard work coming up.
PROMOS:
10 secs:
The nightmare is not over … Firefighters battle to hold the line as wind and dry weather fuel flare-ups of the wild fires that have ravaged the Southern Cape this week.

15 secs:
(8 secs) “Hashtag Cape Storm” became an instant social media “celebrity” in the past week -- but did it bring any real drought relief?
DR PETER JOHNSTON, UNIVERSITY OF CAPE TOWN: We’re hoping that the dams will have filled up maybe 5% in a storm like this. It’s going to take a long time for the dams to fill, it’s not going to happen in one storm.

15 secs:
(9 secs) Fear and panic turned to shock and defeat. Now the thousands who lost their homes in Knysna count the cost and try to work out how to begin again.
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON: We’re all a little overwhelmed. I must say yesterday morning everyone was speechless. This can’t happen.


TITLES:
FRAN KIRSTEN, KNYSNA MUNICIPALITY SPOKESPERSON
LEEROY BAATJIES, SEDGEFIELD FIREFIGHTER
LOUIS JORDAAN, KNYSNA RESIDENT
NIALL O’HAGAN, KNYSNA RESIDENT
DANIELLE PIETERS, OAKHILL SCHOOL EQUESTRIAN CENTRE
CRAIG PATTERSON, KNYSNA RESIDENT
DEE-ANNE OLIVIER, PASTOR
DR PETER JOHNSTON, AFRICAN CLIMATE & DEVELOPMENT INITIATIVE, UCT

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Nine people have died in Cape Town and 3 so far in raging fires around Knysna -- the Defence Force has been called in to help contain the fire and ensure that evacuees are safe. We track the devastatation being left in the wake of the storm - from Cape Town to Knysna and Plettenberg Bay and see how the Cape has rallied to deal with the tragedy of several storm-related deaths.
